content:
Doris "Dorie" Miller (1919-1943) was a U.S. Navy sailor who became one of the first African American heroes of World War II. Here's what I know about him:

## Early Life
- Born October 12, 1919, in Waco, Texas
- Given the name "Doris" but called "Dorie" by family and friends
- One of four sons in a farming family
- Worked on his family's farm and was a football star in high school

## Naval Service
- Enlisted in the U.S. Navy in September 1939
- Due to racial segregation policies, was assigned as a mess attendant (cook) aboard the USS West Virginia
- Despite his assignment, he was known for his physical strength and became the ship's heavyweight boxing champion

## Pearl Harbor Heroism (December 7, 1941)
- Was collecting laundry when the Japanese attack began
- Helped move wounded sailors to safety, including the mortally wounded Captain Mervyn Bennion
- Manned a .50-caliber anti-aircraft machine gun (a weapon he had never been trained to use due to Navy segregation policies)
- Fired at attacking Japanese aircraft until running out of ammunition
- Only abandoned his position when ordered to abandon ship

## Recognition and Legacy
- Awarded the Navy Cross in May 1942 by Admiral Chester Nimitz - the first African American to receive this honor
- His heroism was widely publicized and used in recruitment campaigns
- Promoted to Petty Officer Second Class
- Became a symbol of African American patriotism and courage

## Later Service and Death
- Transferred to other ships and participated in Pacific combat operations
- Killed in action on November 24, 1943, when the USS Liscome Bay was torpedoed by a Japanese submarine during the Battle of Makin
- He was 24 years old

## Posthumous Honors
- Had a destroyer escort (USS Miller) named after him in 1973
- A dining facility at Pearl Harbor bears his name
- Featured on a U.S. postage stamp in 2010
- The Navy announced in 2020 that a Ford-class aircraft carrier would be named USS Doris Miller in his honor

Miller's story represents both heroic service and the contradictions of a segregated military fighting for freedom abroad while denying equal treatment at home.
